faq.a: Lymphoma is painless, firm, and often systemic; TB nodes are matted, may have sinus tracts, and are associated with pulmonary TB signs.
faq.q: How do I differentiate lymphoma from TB lymphadenitis clinically?

faq.a: CBC with differential, ESR/CRP, and HIV rapid test; then ultrasound if available.
faq.q: What is the first test I should order when a patient presents with enlarged nodes?

faq.a: Imaging cannot confirm histology; biopsy provides definitive diagnosis and guides therapy.
faq.q: Why is a biopsy still necessary even if imaging suggests lymphoma?

exam: A 28‑year‑old man with a 3‑month history of painless cervical nodes and night sweats – what is the next best step? — Order HIV test, CBC, ESR, and ultrasound before biopsy; consider lymphoma.
A patient with enlarged nodes and a positive TB PCR – what is the most appropriate management? — Treat TB first, reassess nodes after 2 weeks; if no response, proceed to biopsy.
Why is bleomycin avoided in patients with chronic lung disease? — It can cause severe pulmonary toxicity.
What clinical feature distinguishes lymphoma from a reactive node? — Painless, firm, non‑mobile nodes >2 cm with B symptoms.
When should you refer a patient with lymphadenopathy to oncology? — If nodes are >5 cm, rapidly enlarging, or if biopsy confirms malignancy.
Why might ESR be normal in lymphoma? — In early disease or in patients with anemia of chronic disease; rely on other findings.
What is the role of ultrasound in low‑resource settings? — It helps assess node morphology and guides fine‑needle aspiration when biopsy facilities are limited.
How does HIV infection alter the presentation of lymphoma? — It can mask B symptoms and increase the risk of aggressive subtypes; ART should be started promptly.
ai.title: Lymphoma versus Reactive Lymphadenopathy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Distinguish lymphoma from benign causes of lymph node enlargement using history, exam, basic labs and imaging. Focus on red flags, common tropical infections, and limited tests in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Lymphoma presents as painless, progressive lymphadenopathy, often with systemic symptoms. Reactive nodes are usually tender, transient, and linked to infection or inflammation.
Use the WHO/NIH staging for lymphoma and the 2017 WHO classification. In low‑resource settings, rely on clinical features, basic CBC, ESR, and ultrasound.

t.b: Anemia, leukopenia or leukocytosis; lymphocytosis suggests infection
Elevated in lymphoma but also in infections
Node size, cortical thickness, hilum visibility; loss of hilum suggests malignancy

sections.p: Early recognition prevents complications like tumor lysis syndrome or opportunistic infections. In East Africa, HIV and TB co‑infection are common confounders.

t.b: Positive indicates need for ART and lymphoma risk assessment
Positive suggests TB lymphadenitis; consider anti‑TB therapy before biopsy

sections.p: Ask about night sweats, weight loss, recent infections, travel, and drug use. On exam, note node consistency, mobility, and associated skin changes.
Assuming all painless nodes are malignant; overlooking TB or HIV; ordering CT when ultrasound is adequate; ignoring B symptoms as red flags.
Treat underlying infection first. For confirmed lymphoma, initiate chemotherapy per local protocols (e.g., CHOP). Provide supportive care: transfusions, infection prophylaxis.

t.b: Cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone; avoids bleomycin due to pulmonary risk

sections.p: Normal ESR does not exclude lymphoma; low CD4 count may mask B symptoms; ultrasound may miss small nodes.
Urgent referral if rapid node growth, pain, skin ulceration, or signs of systemic compromise.
